title: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When males and females of a species share the same general habits of life but differ in structure, colour or ornament, those differences were mainly caused by sexual selection, although not all such differences are.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Thus it is, as I believe, that when the males and females of any animal have the same general habits of life, but differ in structure, colour, or ornament, such differences have been mainly caused by sexual selection

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Sexual Selection”. Scope: sexually dimorphic animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Comparative datasets support broad proxy tests of Darwin's historical inference. Ecological selection, sex-specific natural selection and correlated evolution substantially reduce discriminating power.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across animals with similar male and female ecological niches, quantify sexual dimorphism and independent indicators of mate choice or mating competition. A phylogenetically controlled association of dimorphism with sexual-selection intensity, after ecological controls, supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Present-day correlation does not uniquely establish the historical selective cause.

Shared habits and sexual-selection intensity are incompletely coded.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.47
data adequacy: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.64
operationalizability: 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shared habits and structural sex differences can be scored with existing ecological and morphological compilations, but only after a substantial join to sex-specific descriptions. The historical claim that sexual selection was the main cause is harder: the same dimorphism is predicted by niche divergence, predation, and drift. The feasible analysis is a comparative partition for birds and mammals, not a direct reconstruction of cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Restrict the comparison to species whose sexes share diet and foraging stratum, then partition sexual dimorphism into ornamental versus ecological traits and ask which class accounts for more of the sex difference. Ornament-dominated dimorphism would support a mainly sexual-selection reading; ecological dimorphism in those same species would count against it. Causation remains an inference from the partition.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Calling a trait an ornament already leans on the sexual-selection hypothesis.

Niche similarity between sexes is coarsely coded.

Most global trait tables are not sex-specific, so ornament dimorphism must be joined from scattered sources.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.54
discriminating power: 0.44
data adequacy: 0.42
data existence: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.54
